data.content_ref: inline:The mechanism claim that a large service can enforce 'Byzantine fault tolerance' or 'n-version programming' at the system level conflates two fundamentally different mechanisms, and neither rescues the claim from its own counterconditions. N-version programming is explicitly faulted by the empirical literature (Knight & Leveson, 1986) for NOT delivering independence — independently developed versions still exhibit correlated faults because of shared problem-domain misconceptions. By invoking n-version programming as the mechanism ensuring 'independent implementations fail independently,' the target rests its case on a technique whose own track record exemplifies the very correlated-failure problem the question asks us to distinguish. The covering principle the target seeks — enforced diversity breaking correlation — is not established by naming BFT or n-version programming; BFT tolerates Byzantine behavior via voting and redundancy in numbers, not via true failure independence, and thus does not guarantee the 'strictly more internal redundancy → more resilient' chain the claim asserts.
